prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part, B001 with Katori and Ye, and the first round has strengthened it. Six of eight files name the same two laureates, but I do not rely on that count. The scientific case is that Katori's magic-wavelength lattice solved a specific problem, namely how to interrogate thousands of neutral atoms without Doppler, recoil or first-order light-shift limits, and that Ye's group turned the idea into the strontium systems that reached 10^-18 and into clock-comparison and many-body clock physics. Independent laboratories (RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) agree at that level, so the result does not rest on one group's claim. Two names map onto two decisive contributions, concept and record realisation, which is not true of any other shortlisted candidate. In answer to the chair's question on timing, I regard demonstrated and independently reproduced 10^-18 performance as sufficient; the redefinition of the second is supporting context and should not be made a condition. The citation should name the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength concept explicitly, so that it is visibly distinct from the 2005 comb prize, where the comb is the readout tool, and from the 2012 prize on quantum control of single ions.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. The 1989, 2005 and 2012 prizes sit in the same neighbourhood, and a critic can call this a third prize for precision spectroscopy; I treat that as a presentational point because the lattice clock is a distinct invention, but I do not dismiss it. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, the Yb groups and the ion-clock community are outside the two names, and the committee should say openly that two names cannot cover the whole clock community. Finally, the practical payoffs (a redefined second, a variation of constants, a dark-sector signal) are still prospective, so the prize would honour a demonstrated measurement capability and not an observed new effect.

responses.point: Kroll supports B001 with Katori and Ye, treats the 2005 and 2012 overlap as presentational, and flags a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory as a possible recusal issue on B001.
responses.response: I agree with the first part: the overlap is a matter of wording and not a bar. On the disclosure, I see the stay in Boulder as a tradition-level link and not a tie to Katori or Ye, so I would discount rather than recuse. I would also ask that the citation say what Ye's group added beyond the comb heritage, namely the 10^-18 strontium systems and clock-comparison work, so that the credit does not read as a second prize for the comb. If Kroll wants his B001 weight discounted for transparency, I would not object, because the support for B001 does not depend on one vote.

responses.point: Pearce puts B001 first but adds B027 (IceCube, Halzen alone) as a second part to spread the award across fields, and says he would drop to B001 alone if colleagues find the single-name credit unconvincing.
responses.response: I welcome his statement that B001 alone is cleaner, and I take him up on it. I accept that the diffuse flux is established and that neutrino astronomy is a real new window, but a one-name part for a collaboration of hundreds is exposed, and the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 associations are still at moderate significance, so the case is a few years from maturity. Adding a weaker second part would dilute a configuration that the committee already accepts. Spreading across fields is not a scientific argument for a part, so I would keep IceCube for a later year, with a configuration that credits the proposers and builders as well.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) and argues that the unsettled pairing mechanism is a separate question from the merit of the discovery, but concedes that B001 is cleaner on attribution.
responses.response: The comparison with high-temperature superconductivity is fair as to merit: an open mechanism does not undo an experimental discovery. My difficulty is attribution and field maturity, not mechanism. Cao, the first author of the decisive 2018 experiments, and Dean, Young, Yacoby and Efetov are outside the three names, and relying on a group-leader convention for the experiment is something I would prefer to avoid when a cleaner alternative exists. His own concession that B001 is cleaner on attribution is the point that decides it for me this year. I would be ready to look at B017 again once reproduction across laboratories and stacks has shown which results are robust, and I would not accept it as a second part now unless the committee could settle the credit for Cao and the experimental groups, which I do not think it can.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B017 first as the cleanest theory-to-experiment story and proposes to state openly that experimental credit goes to the group through its leader, saying he cannot judge the lattice clock from outside the field.
responses.response: I share his admiration for the prediction followed by experiment, and the clean mapping of three names is a real strength. I disagree on how much the open-credit statement can carry. It works as a footnote when the omissions are peripheral, but here the first author of the discovery paper is outside the list. Since he cannot judge the clock field, I would add that the clock result is easier to check from outside than most: several national laboratories measured it independently, and the 10^-18 figure is a number, not an interpretation. I keep B017 as my first alternative, not as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 1989, 2005 and 2012 prizes as a bar rather than a presentational point; I think not, but I cannot exclude that others will weigh it more heavily.
How the citation should best split credit between Katori's magic-wavelength concept and Ye's record-accuracy realisation, and whether the word realisation or co-invention is fairer to both.
Whether contributors outside the two names (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others) can be set aside without unfairness; this cannot be settled from the shortlist alone.
My recollection of the detailed history of the clocks and of twisted bilayer graphene is from memory and not verified against sources.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye, and my co-authors and institutions do not overlap with the B001 candidates. I do not teach or work in the clock field. After reading the round-1 disclosures I see no reason to change this, and I note that Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and the chair have disclosed proximity of various kinds, which the committee should weigh as it sees fit.
